claim: Only about a third of field-collected Dictyostelium discoideum amoebae carry a symbiont.
source: Only about a third of field-collected amoebae carry a symbiont.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a direct observation from field collections.

claim: Before curing, field-collected D. discoideum clones did not vary significantly in overall fitness.
source: Before curing, field-collected clones did not vary significantly in overall fitness, but infected hosts produced morphologically different multicellular structures.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results from the abstract.

claim: Before curing, infected D. discoideum hosts produced morphologically different multicellular structures.
source: Before curing, field-collected clones did not vary significantly in overall fitness, but infected hosts produced morphologically different multicellular structures.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results from the abstract.

claim: After curing and reinfecting, D. discoideum host fitness declined.
source: After curing and reinfecting, host fitness declined.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results from the abstract.

claim: Natural B. hayleyella hosts suffered fewer fitness costs when reinfected with B. hayleyella.
source: However, natural B. hayleyella hosts suffered fewer fitness costs when reinfected with B. hayleyella, indicating that they have evolved mechanisms to tolerate their symbiont.
evidence: This is a direct statement of experimental results from the abstract.

claim: Natural B. hayleyella hosts have evolved mechanisms to tolerate their symbiont.
source: However, natural B. hayleyella hosts suffered fewer fitness costs when reinfected with B. hayleyella, indicating that they have evolved mechanisms to tolerate their symbiont.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fitness data presented in the abstract.

claim: Mutualisms arise when different parties can contribute unique abilities or resources to one another, under conditions where exploitation is controlled.
source: Mutualisms arise when different parties can contribute unique abilities or resources to one another, under conditions where exploitation is controlled (Bronstein, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bronstein, 2015.

claim: Symbioses are rife with potential conflict.
source: Symbioses are rife with potential conflict (Dale and Moran, 2006; Estrela et al., 2016; Garcia and Gerardo, 2014; Moran, 2007; Oliver et al., 2005).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Symbiotic relationships are pervasive and persistent.
source: Despite this, symbiotic relationships are pervasive and persistent (Douglas, 2008; Moran et al., 1993; Wernegreen, 2017; Werner et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: The stability and ubiquity of symbiotic interactions implies that conflict can be managed or minimized by partners over multiple generations.
source: The stability and ubiquity of these interactions implies that conflict can be managed or minimized by partners over multiple generations.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of stable symbioses.

claim: Examining extant symbiotic associations may not reveal the underlying mutualism to parasitism continuum that drives evolutionary change.
source: Recent studies suggest that examining extant symbiotic associations may not reveal the underlying mutualism to parasitism continuum that drives evolutionary change (Moran, 2007; Queller and Strassmann, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Moran, 2007 and Queller and Strassmann, 2018.

claim: The view that symbiotic associations fluctuate along a mutualism-to-parasitism continuum is increasingly appreciated.
source: Indeed, the view that symbiotic associations fluctuate along a mutualism-to-parasitism continuum is increasingly appreciated (McFall-Ngai et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to McFall-Ngai et al., 2013.

claim: Mutualistic endosymbionts evolve specialized lifestyles that parallel those of intracellular pathogens.
source: To exploit their host niche, mutualistic endosymbionts evolve specialized lifestyles that parallel those of intracellular pathogens (Casadevall, 2008; McCutcheon and Moran, 2011; Soto et al., 2009).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Some endosymbionts become beneficial or even obligate for host survival.
source: Despite initial exploitative strategies, some endosymbionts become beneficial or even obligate for host survival, a situation common for many insect nutritional endosymbioses (Douglas, 2009).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Douglas, 2009.

claim: Strict vertical transmission of endosymbionts typically promotes a more tranquil relationship as the evolutionary fates of the two parties become increasingly interdependent.
source: Strict vertical transmission of endosymbionts typically promotes a more tranquil relationship as the evolutionary fates of the two parties become increasingly interdependent (Ferdy and Godelle, 2005; Hosokawa et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Ferdy and Godelle, 2005 and Hosokawa et al., 2016.

claim: Host dependency often leads to the reduction in size of symbiont genomes as they become more streamlined for life within their host.
source: Host dependency also often leads to the reduction in size of symbiont genomes as they become more streamlined for life within their host, something true for both beneficial and pathogenic endosymbionts (Dale and Moran, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Dale and Moran, 2006.

claim: Horizontally acquired facultative symbionts are more likely to retain active conflicts.
source: Horizontally acquired facultative symbionts are more likely to retain active conflicts.
evidence: This is stated as a general principle in the introduction.

claim: Manipulating the jellyfish symbiont Symbiodinium microadriaticum towards solely vertical or horizontal transmission modes led to the evolution of more mutualistic or parasitic lineages respectively.
source: This has been experimentally demonstrated by manipulating the jellyfish symbiont Symbiodinium microadriaticum towards solely vertical or horizontal transmission modes, leading to the evolution of more mutualistic or parasitic lineages respectively (Sachs and Wilcox, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Sachs and Wilcox, 2006.

claim: Horizontal transmission can favor symbionts that behave more parasitically.
source: Though horizontal transmission can favor symbionts that behave more parasitically, selection can favor hosts that employ more severe countermeasures to limit symbiont entry or growth (Nyholm and McFall-Ngai, 2004; Ratzka et al., 2012; Reynolds and Rolff, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Selection can favor hosts that employ more severe countermeasures to limit symbiont entry or growth.
source: Though horizontal transmission can favor symbionts that behave more parasitically, selection can favor hosts that employ more severe countermeasures to limit symbiont entry or growth (Nyholm and McFall-Ngai, 2004; Ratzka et al., 2012; Reynolds and Rolff, 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Paramecium bursaria can manipulate its facultative nutritional symbiont (Chlorella sp.) in a relationship that provides no apparent benefit for the imprisoned symbiont.
source: Indeed, host-driven control can be extreme, as demonstrated by the ability of Paramecium bursaria to manipulate its facultative nutritional symbiont (Chlorella sp.) in a relationship that provides no apparent benefit for the imprisoned symbiont (Lowe et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Lowe et al., 2016.

claim: Symbiotic relationships may be positive or negative under different environmental conditions.
source: Symbiotic relationships may be positive or negative under different environmental conditions (Leung and Poulin, 2008; Pérez-Brocal et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Leung and Poulin, 2008 and Pérez-Brocal et al., 2011.

claim: H. defensa infection confers host resistance to parasitoid attack in Acyrthosiphon pisum.
source: H. defensa infection confers host resistance to parasitoid attack, with resistance being greater for hosts co-infected with Serratia symbiotica (Oliver et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oliver et al., 2006.

claim: Co-infection of Acyrthosiphon pisum with H. defensa and Serratia symbiotica comes at a high fecundity cost.
source: However, co-infection comes at a high fecundity cost, such that in parasitoid free environments, host fitness is reduced compared to uninfected counterparts (Oliver et al., 2006).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Oliver et al., 2006.

claim: During the unicellular stage, D. discoideum amoebae consume bacteria by phagocytosis and divide.
source: During the unicellular stage, amoebae consume bacteria by phagocytosis and divide.
evidence: This is a description of the D. discoideum life cycle based on established knowledge.

claim: When prey are scarce, D. discoideum amoebae aggregate by tens of thousands to form multicellular slugs.
source: When prey are scarce, amoebae aggregate by tens of thousands to form multicellular slugs that move towards heat and light, seeking out a location to form fruiting bodies.
evidence: This is a description of the D. discoideum life cycle based on established knowledge.

claim: D. discoideum fruiting bodies consist of a stalk of sacrificial dead cells which support a globular sorus containing hardy spore cells.
source: These fruiting bodies consist of a stalk of sacrificial dead cells which support a globular sorus containing hardy spore cells (Kessin, 2001).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Kessin, 2001.

claim: Processes employed by specialized immune-like cells (sentinel cells) during slug migration and fruiting body formation remove any remaining bacteria, typically producing bacteria-free sori.
source: Processes employed by specialized immune-like cells (sentinel cells) during slug migration and fruiting body formation remove any remaining bacteria, typically producing bacteria-free sori (Brock et al., 2011; Chen et al., 2007; Cosson and Lima, 2014).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations.

claim: Some D. discoideum isolates harvested from the wild are infected with Burkholderia symbionts.
source: However, some D. discoideum isolates harvested from the wild are infected with Burkholderia symbionts (Brock et al., 2011).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brock et al., 2011.

claim: Burkholderia infection persists in the lab throughout the social cycle, where intracellular bacteria can be visualized within spores and sori.
source: Infection persists in the lab throughout the social cycle, where intracellular bacteria can be visualized within spores and sori (DiSalvo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to DiSalvo et al., 2015.

claim: Burkholderia infection can be terminated by treating hosts with antibiotics.
source: Infection can be terminated by treating hosts with antibiotics and induced by exposing naïve hosts to Burkholderia, thereby allowing us to easily mix and match partners and study subsequent fitness consequences (Brock et al., 2016a; DiSalvo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brock et al., 2016a and DiSalvo et al., 2015.

claim: Burkholderia infection can be induced by exposing naïve D. discoideum hosts to Burkholderia.
source: Infection can be terminated by treating hosts with antibiotics and induced by exposing naïve hosts to Burkholderia, thereby allowing us to easily mix and match partners and study subsequent fitness consequences (Brock et al., 2016a; DiSalvo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brock et al., 2016a and DiSalvo et al., 2015.

claim: D. discoideum has a meiotic sexual process that occurs much less frequently than the asexual proliferation process of binary fission.
source: D. discoideum also has a meiotic sexual process, that occurs much less frequently than the asexual proliferation process of binary fission that amoebae go through every few hours (Bloomfield et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Bloomfield et al., 2010.

claim: Under standard laboratory growth conditions, Burkholderia infection is detrimental for D. discoideum hosts because it decreases slug migration and spore production.
source: Under standard laboratory growth conditions, Burkholderia infection is detrimental for hosts because it decreases slug migration and spore production (Brock et al., 2016a; DiSalvo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brock et al., 2016a and DiSalvo et al., 2015.

claim: Burkholderia infection induces secondary carriage of edible bacteria, which can increase host fitness in food scarce conditions.
source: Infection induces secondary carriage of edible bacteria (Burkholderia is typically inedible), which can increase host fitness in food scarce conditions when the carried food bacteria reseed new environments with a food source (Brock et al., 2011; DiSalvo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Brock et al., 2011 and DiSalvo et al., 2015.

claim: Burkholderia is typically inedible to D. discoideum.
source: Infection induces secondary carriage of edible bacteria (Burkholderia is typically inedible), which can increase host fitness in food scarce conditions when the carried food bacteria reseed new environments with a food source (Brock et al., 2011; DiSalvo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is stated in the text and supported by citations.

claim: Infected D. discoideum hosts are less harmed by ethidium bromide exposure, possibly mediated by bacterial degradation of the toxin.
source: Additionally, infected hosts are less harmed by ethidium bromide exposure, possibly mediated by bacterial degradation of the toxin (Brock et al., 2016a).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brock et al., 2016a, with speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Three Burkholderia species have been identified associated with Dictyostelium: B. agricolaris, B. hayleyella, and B. bonniea.
source: We have identified three Burkholderia species associated with Dictyostelium: B. agricolaris, B. hayleyella, and B. bonniea (Brock et al., 2018).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to Brock et al., 2018.

claim: B. agricolaris and B. hayleyella differentially impact D. discoideum host fitness.
source: Most of our work has been conducted with the first two species, which differentially impact host fitness.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a general observation.

claim: B. hayleyella is most detrimental for D. discoideum hosts in general.
source: We find that B. hayleyella is most detrimental for D. discoideum hosts in general, but is most costly to those first exposed to it in the lab.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the results.

claim: B. hayleyella is most costly to D. discoideum hosts first exposed to it in the lab.
source: We find that B. hayleyella is most detrimental for D. discoideum hosts in general, but is most costly to those first exposed to it in the lab.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the results.

claim: Both B. agricolaris and B. hayleyella can be observed within phagocytic vacuoles in D. discoideum.
source: Although both species of bacteria can be observed within phagocytic vacuoles, B. hayleyella infects more cells and damages fruiting body structures.
evidence: This is a summary statement of microscopy observations.

claim: B. hayleyella infects more D. discoideum cells than B. agricolaris.
source: Although both species of bacteria can be observed within phagocytic vacuoles, B. hayleyella infects more cells and damages fruiting body structures.
evidence: This is a summary statement of microscopy observations.

claim: B. hayleyella damages D. discoideum fruiting body structures.
source: Although both species of bacteria can be observed within phagocytic vacuoles, B. hayleyella infects more cells and damages fruiting body structures.
evidence: This is a summary statement of microscopy observations.

claim: Morphological aberrations caused by B. hayleyella are less severe in native-hayleyella hosts.
source: These morphological aberrations are also less severe in native-hayleyella hosts, suggesting that native hosts have evolved mechanisms to withstand symbiont colonization.
evidence: This is a summary statement of microscopy observations with an inference about evolution.

claim: Native-hayleyella hosts have evolved mechanisms to withstand symbiont colonization.
source: These morphological aberrations are also less severe in native-hayleyella hosts, suggesting that native hosts have evolved mechanisms to withstand symbiont colonization.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation of less severe morphological aberrations.

claim: Infection status in the field did not affect total viable spore counts for naïve, native-agricolaris, or native-hayleyella D. discoideum hosts.
source: We found that infection status in the field did not affect total viable spore counts for naïve, native-agricolaris, or native-hayleyella hosts (Figure 2a and Supplementary file 1a) (linear mixed model (LMM), ΔAIC = −1.57, χ2 = 5.57, DF = 2, p = 0.062).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 2a.

claim: Field-infected native D. discoideum hosts do not seem to suffer any net fitness costs from infection by the measure of viable spore production.
source: Thus, field-infected native hosts do not seem to suffer any net fitness costs from infection by this measure.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the statistical results on viable spore production.

claim: Wild-collected D. discoideum hosts did not experience lowered fitness after being cured with antibiotics.
source: We found that wild-collected hosts of our three categories did not experience lowered fitness after being cured with antibiotics (Figure 2a and b) (viable spore production: LMM, ΔAIC = 1.74, χ2 = 2.26, DF = 2, p = 0.32, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Antibiotic treatment increased viable spore production of native-agricolaris hosts compared to uncured native-agricolaris hosts.
source: Antibiotic treatment actually increased viable spore production of native-agricolaris hosts compared to uncured native-agricolaris hosts (LMM, ΔAIC = −5.68, χ2 = 9.68, DF = 2, p = 0.008; Figure 2a and b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 2.

claim: There was an overall effect on total spore viability with the addition of Burkholderia to all antibiotic-cured D. discoideum hosts.
source: We found an overall effect on total spore viability with the addition of Burkholderia to all antibiotic-cured hosts (LMM, ΔAIC = −198.81, χ2 = 210.81, DF = 6, P ≪ 0.001).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: Addition of B. agricolaris to cured D. discoideum hosts decreased their fitness.
source: Addition of either B. agricolaris (Wald t = −10.19, DF = 96, P ≪ 0.001) or B. hayleyella (t = −13.58, DF = 96, P ≪ 0.001) to any of the cured hosts decreased their fitness (Figure 2; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Addition of B. hayleyella to cured D. discoideum hosts decreased their fitness.
source: Addition of either B. agricolaris (Wald t = −10.19, DF = 96, P ≪ 0.001) or B. hayleyella (t = −13.58, DF = 96, P ≪ 0.001) to any of the cured hosts decreased their fitness (Figure 2; Supplementary file 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The addition of B. hayleyella to D. discoideum led to significantly lower viable spore production than did the addition of B. agricolaris.
source: Overall, the addition of B. hayleyella to D. discoideum led to significantly lower viable spore production than did the addition of B. agricolaris (Wald t = −4.48, DF = 96, P ≪ 0.001) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 2.

claim: There was an interaction effect between native host status and which Burkholderia species was added on total viable spore production.
source: There was an interaction effect on total viable spore production (LMM, ΔAIC = −199.93, χ2 = 215.92, DF = 8, P ≪ 0.001) (Supplementary file 2e).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: When B. hayleyella was added to the three cured hosts, native-hayleyella hosts had higher fitness than did either native-agricolaris or naïve hosts.
source: When B. hayleyella was added to the three cured hosts, native-hayleyella hosts had higher fitness than did either native-agricolaris or naïve hosts (both P ≪ 0.001, Figure 2d; Supplementary file 2e).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 2d.

claim: Native-agricolaris hosts did not have significantly higher fitness with the addition of B. agricolaris than either native-hayleyella or naïve hosts.
source: In contrast, native-agricolaris hosts did not have significantly higher fitness with the addition of B. agricolaris than either native-hayleyella or naïve hosts (both p > 0.05, (Figure 2c; Supplementary 2e).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 2c.

claim: Native-hayleyella hosts are adapted to colonization by their field-acquired symbionts.
source: These results indicate that native-hayleyella hosts are adapted to colonization by their field-acquired symbionts.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the fitness data showing native-hayleyella hosts do better with B. hayleyella.

claim: D. discoideum morphology without Burkholderia in both naïve and cured native hosts has vegetative cells that harbor no intracellular bacteria but contain many empty multilamellar bodies inside vacuoles.
source: D. discoideum morphology without Burkholderia in both naïve and cured native hosts, has vegetative cells that harbor no intracellular bacteria but contain many empty multilamellar bodies inside vacuoles (Figure 3a and Figure 3–figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 3a.

claim: Multilamellar bodies are predominantly composed of amoebae membranes and are thought to be a byproduct of bacterial digestion.
source: Multilamellar bodies are predominantly composed of amoebae membranes and are thought to be a byproduct of bacterial digestion as they are produced when amoebae are fed bacterial food (Denoncourt et al., 2016; Paquet et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Denoncourt et al., 2016 and Paquet et al., 2013.

claim: Confocal microscopy of vegetative amoebae from uninfected hosts grown with GFP-labeled food bacteria contain little to no intracellular GFP, suggesting that they have digested food bacteria by the time of fixation.
source: Confocal microscopy of vegetative amoebae from this same host set grown with GFP-labeled food bacteria (K. pneumoniae) contain little to no intracellular GFP, suggesting that they have digested food bacteria by the time of fixation (Figure 4a).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 4a and an inference about digestion.

claim: No intact bacteria were found in naïve or cured native D. discoideum host slugs.
source: In accordance with our observations that all bacteria were killed and digested by vegetative cells, we found no intact bacteria in naïve or cured native host slugs (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 5a.

claim: Slug cells from uninfected D. discoideum were in general compacted with electron dense materials and contained no vacuoles or multi-lamellar bodies.
source: In addition, slug cells were in general compacted with electron dense materials and contained no vacuoles or multi-lamellar bodies (Figure 5a).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 5a.

claim: Bacteria were not detected in stalk cells or spores of uninfected D. discoideum fruiting bodies.
source: In uninfected fruiting bodies, we did not detect bacteria in stalk cells or spores (Figures 6a and 7a).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figures 6a and 7a.

claim: Spores from uninfected D. discoideum were packed with electron dense materials with no food vacuoles or multi-lamellar bodies.
source: Instead spores were packed with electron dense materials with no food vacuoles or multi-lamellar bodies (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 6a.

claim: Stalk cells from uninfected D. discoideum showed plant cell-like characteristics, having a cellulosic cell wall and containing a single large vacuole.
source: Stalk cells showed plant cell-like characteristics, having a cellulosic cell wall and containing a single large vacuole (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 6a.

claim: Inside the large vacuole of uninfected D. discoideum stalk cells, there were some mitochondria and other cellular materials but no bacteria.
source: Inside the large vacuole, there were some mitochondria and other cellular materials but no bacteria (Figure 6a).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 6a.

claim: The food bacterium K. pneumoniae was efficiently cleared during the social cycle from amoebae uninfected by Burkholderia and the amoebae then aggregate and produce bacteria-free fruiting bodies.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that the food bacterium we used, Klebsiella pneumoniae, was efficiently cleared during the social cycle from amoebae uninfected by Burkholderia and the amoebae then aggregate and produce bacteria-free fruiting bodies.
evidence: This is an inference based on the microscopy observations of uninfected hosts.

claim: When D. discoideum is infected with Burkholderia, Burkholderia is found in amoebae, slug cells, spores, and stalk cells.
source: When D. discoideum is infected with Burkholderia, we find it in amoebae, slug cells, spores, and stalk cells.
evidence: This is a summary statement of microscopy observations.

claim: Using confocal microscopy and RFP labeled Burkholderia strains, high levels of Burkholderia were identified inside host amoebae.
source: Using confocal microscopy and RFP labeled Burkholderia strains, we were able to specifically identify high levels of Burkholderia inside host amoebae (Figure 4b,c).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 4b,c.

claim: B. hayleyella was present in more of the amoebae than B. agricolaris was.
source: B. hayleyella was present in more of the amoebae than B. agricolaris was (Figure 4b,c).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 4b,c.

claim: The higher number of B. hayleyella bacteria may account for the more detrimental fitness consequences it imposes.
source: The higher number of B. hayleyella bacteria may account for the more detrimental fitness consequences it imposes (Figure 2).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of higher bacterial numbers and fitness data.

claim: The food bacterium K. pneumoniae labelled with GFP was occasionally observed in Burkholderia infected amoebae, particularly those infected by B. agricolaris.
source: The food bacterium K. pneumoniae labelled with GFP was occasionally observed in Burkholderia infected amoebae, particularly those infected by B. agricolaris (Figures 4b and 7b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figures 4b and 7b.

claim: Burkholderia colonization may partially impede food digestion, thereby allowing co-colonization of secondary bacteria and contributing to the proto-farming phenotype.
source: This suggests that Burkholderia colonization may partially impede food digestion, thereby allowing co-colonization of secondary bacteria and contributing to the proto-farming phenotype (Brock et al., 2011; DiSalvo et al., 2015).
evidence: This is speculation based on the observation of co-colonization, supported by citations.

claim: Burkholderia are much more abundant in amoebae than are K. pneumoniae.
source: However, confocal images demonstrate that Burkholderia are much more abundant in amoebae than are K. pneumoniae, indicating that the majority of intact intracellular bacteria observed via transmission electron microscopy (TEM) are most likely Burkholderia cells (Figures 3, 5 and 6).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figures 3, 5 and 6.

claim: TEM of vegetative amoebae shows intact bacteria which are inferred to be Burkholderia surrounded by multi-lamellar bodies and located inside what appear to be food vacuoles.
source: TEM of vegetative amoebae shows intact bacteria which we infer to be Burkholderia surrounded by multi-lamellar bodies and located inside what appear to be food vacuoles (Figure 3b,c).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 3b,c.

claim: The undamaged appearance of Burkholderia in food vacuoles suggests that they are resistant to phagocytic digestion.
source: Their undamaged appearance suggests that they are resistant to phagocytic digestion.
evidence: This is an inference based on the microscopy observations.

claim: Empty multi-lamellar bodies are observed inside food vacuoles of infected amoebae, suggesting that digestion is not completely arrested during colonization.
source: In addition to the presence of intact intracellular bacteria, we also observe empty multi-lamellar bodies inside food vacuoles of infected amoebae. This suggests that digestion is not completely arrested during colonization, an unsurprising finding given that hosts continue to grow and multiply.
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with an inference about digestion.

claim: Multi-lamellar bodies containing intact bacteria were not found secreted into the extracellular environment, indicating that Burkholderia may not be expelled from host cells via multi-lamellar body excretion.
source: Interestingly, we did not find multi-lamellar bodies containing intact bacteria secreted into the extracellular environment, indicating that Burkholderia may not be expelled from host cells via multi-lamellar body excretion.
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with an inference about bacterial expulsion.

claim: In Burkholderia infected hosts, intact bacteria are retained in food vacuoles throughout the transition to multicellular slugs.
source: In Burkholderia infected hosts, intact bacteria are retained in food vacuoles throughout the transition to multicellular slugs, suggesting that bacteria stay within phagosomes throughout the aggregation stage (Figure 5b,c).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 5b,c.

claim: No obvious morphological defects were detected in infected slugs or differences between slugs infected with different Burkholderia species through TEM.
source: Through TEM, we did not detect obvious morphological defects in infected slugs or differences between slugs infected with different Burkholderia species.
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations.

claim: After fruiting body development, intracellular bacteria are found in both stalk and spore cells of Burkholderia infected hosts.
source: After fruiting body development, we find intracellular bacteria in both stalk and spore cells of Burkholderia infected hosts (Figure 6b,c).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 6b,c.

claim: In infected stalk cells, intact bacteria reside in single large vacuoles inside the cellulosic cell wall.
source: In infected stalk cells, intact bacteria reside in single large vacuoles inside the cellulosic cell wall (Figure 6b,c).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 6b,c.

claim: In spore cells, bacteria remain within vacuoles.
source: In spore cells, bacteria remain within vacuoles (Figure 6b,c).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 6b,c.

claim: Bacterial cells were observed outside spores but within the sorus, suggesting that bacteria may be carried interstitially into fruiting body structures, or they may be escaping pre-spore or spore cells within the sorus.
source: We also observed bacterial cells outside spores but within the sorus, suggesting that bacteria may be carried interstitially into fruiting body structures, or they may be escaping pre-spore or spore cells within the sorus (Figure 7b,c).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 7b,c and speculation about the mechanism.

claim: Strikingly altered morphologies were not observed for B. agricolaris infected spore and stalk cells.
source: We did not observe strikingly altered morphologies for B. agricolaris infected spore and stalk cells (Figure 6b).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 6b.

claim: The spore and stalk cells of naïve hosts infected with B. hayleyella appeared to be morphologically aberrant.
source: However, the spore and stalk cells of naïve hosts infected with B. hayleyella appeared to be morphologically aberrant (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 6c.

claim: Numerous broken spores and signs that bacterial cells were escaping from damaged spores were found in naïve hosts infected with B. hayleyella.
source: We found numerous broken spores and signs that bacterial cells were escaping from damaged spores (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 6c.

claim: The whole stalk structure was often collapsed and filled with bacteria in naïve hosts infected with B. hayleyella.
source: In addition, the whole stalk structure was often collapsed and filled with bacteria (Figure 6c).
evidence: This is a direct statement of microscopy observations with reference to Figure 6c.

claim: No clear cellulosic cell wall was observed in stalk cells of naïve hosts infected with B. hayleyella, suggesting that B. hayleyella colonization inhibits the normal development of stalk cells or results in their disruption in naïve hosts and native-agricolaris hosts.
